messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Threat

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Fatima is a 51-year-old divorced woman of Lebanese descent who works as a social ministry worker in a mid-sized city in the American Midwest. She came to the intake appointment alone, though she had rescheduled twice before finally arriving, and she seated herself immediately adjacent to the office door — a habit, she explained quietly, that she no longer questions. She has a PCL-5 score of 62, and the history she offered across the first two sessions was fragmentary, delivered in pieces she seemed to retrieve with physical effort.

The trauma Fatima carries is not a single event but a sustained architecture of harm that began in early childhood. Her primary caregiver — her father — was physically violent throughout her formative years, and the violence was unpredictable in its timing but consistent in its character: she would be struck from behind, from the side, without warning, often while her back was turned. The blows came when she was seated, when she was crouching, when she was cornered. The body learned what the mind could not articulate. Decades later, Fatima cannot describe what happened in any coherent narrative sequence. When she tries to put the experience into words, the language dissolves. What remains instead is sensory and somatic — a tightening across the shoulders, a bracing in the lower back, a posture of anticipatory collapse that her body reassumes without her permission when the memories surface. She described sitting in a staff meeting last autumn and feeling, without any identifiable trigger, that her spine had curved inward, that her arms had come up. Her colleague asked if she was cold. She said yes. When the memories come, they also bring rage — not grief, not fear, but a white and disorienting fury that she finds more frightening than the sadness she expected. She has no framework for it.

Because the memories arrive without warning and carry such physical and emotional force, Fatima has developed a set of strategies that began as reasonable precautions and have since become the scaffolding of her daily life. She avoids being alone with any other person in an enclosed space — a rule she maintains with quiet vigilance at work, where her ministry role requires home visits and one-on-one client meetings. She has declined several case assignments over the past year, citing scheduling conflicts, and her supervisor has begun to notice. She ensures she is always near an exit — in the office, in waiting rooms, in the church hall where her ministry team holds community meals. She has, without announcing it, reorganized her entire spatial relationship to every room she enters. She has also, with increasing frequency, simply avoided going to work at all, calling in on mornings when the anticipatory dread becomes too heavy. These absences have cost her professionally and have deepened her sense of isolation.

The threat she perceives in ordinary environments is constant and exhausting. She is frequently irritable — snapping at colleagues who approach her desk from behind, raising her voice in ways she later regrets — and she has come to believe, with a certainty that embarrasses her, that she is simply dangerous to be around. She checks behind her when she walks down the corridor at work, scanning for footsteps. She reacts to a door closing too loudly as though something has been launched at her. This sustained state of alarm feeds directly back into the memories: when her body is already primed, already scanning, the somatic fragments return more readily, and the rage that accompanies them feels less like a symptom and more like evidence of something broken in her. The checking and the avoidance keep her nervous system in a register where the past feels present, which in turn makes the memories more intrusive, which makes the threat feel more real, which makes the exits more necessary.

What finally brought Fatima to seek help was a morning three months ago when she sat in her car in the ministry parking lot for forty minutes, unable to go inside, certain — without reason she could name — that something terrible was waiting for her in the building where she has worked for eleven years. She drove home. She did not call in. She sat in her apartment until dark. What she is most afraid of, she said at the end of the second session, is that this is simply who she is now. What she is most hoping for is that it isn't.
